sourceExcerptReferences.greek: Ἡροδότου Ἁλικαρνησσέος ἱστορίης ἀπόδεξις ἥδε, ὡς μήτε τὰ γενόμενα ἐξ ἀνθρώπων τῷ χρόνῳ ἐξίτηλα γένηται, μήτε ἔργα μεγάλα τε καὶ θωμαστά, τὰ μὲν Ἕλλησι τὰ δὲ βαρβάροισι ἀποδεχθέντα, ἀκλεᾶ γένηται, τά τε ἄλλα καὶ διʼ ἣν αἰτίην ἐπολέμησαν ἀλλήλοισι.

Περσέων μέν νυν οἱ λόγιοι Φοίνικας αἰτίους φασὶ γενέσθαι τῆς διαφορῆς. τούτους γὰρ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἐρυθρῆς καλεομένης θαλάσσης ἀπικομένους ἐπὶ τήνδε τὴν θάλασσαν, καὶ οἰκήσαντας τοῦτον τὸν χῶρον τὸν καὶ νῦν οἰκέουσι, αὐτίκα ναυτιλίῃσι μακρῇσι ἐπιθέσθαι, ἀπαγινέοντας δὲ φορτία Αἰγύπτιά τε καὶ Ἀσσύρια τῇ τε ἄλλῃ ἐσαπικνέεσθαι καὶ δὴ καὶ ἐς Ἄργος.
τὸ δὲ Ἄργος τοῦτον τὸν χρόνον προεῖχε ἅπασι τῶν ἐν τῇ νῦν Ἑλλάδι καλεομένῃ χωρῇ. ἀπικομένους δὲ τούς Φοίνικας ἐς δὴ τὸ Ἄργος τοῦτο διατίθεσθαι τὸν φόρτον.

πέμπτῃ δὲ ἢ ἕκτῃ ἡμέρῃ ἀπʼ ἧς ἀπίκοντο, ἐξεμπολημένων σφι σχεδόν πάντων, ἐλθεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν γυναῖκας ἄλλας τε πολλάς καὶ δὴ καὶ τοῦ βασιλέος θυγατέρα· τὸ δέ οἱ οὔνομα εἶναι, κατὰ τὠυτὸ τὸ καὶ Ἕλληνές λέγουσι, Ἰοῦν τὴν Ἰνάχου·

ταύτας στάσας κατά πρύμνην τῆς νεὸς ὠνέεσθαι τῶν φορτίων τῶν σφι ἦν θυμός μάλιστα· καὶ τοὺς Φοίνικας διακελευσαμένους ὁρμῆσαι ἐπʼ αὐτάς. τὰς μὲν δὴ πλεῦνας τῶν γυναικῶν ἀποφυγεῖν, τὴν δὲ Ἰοῦν σὺν ἄλλῃσι ἁρπασθῆναι. ἐσβαλομένους δὲ ἐς τὴν νέα οἴχεσθαι ἀποπλέοντας ἐπʼ Αἰγύπτου.

literalTranslations.translation: This is the presentation of the inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassus: so that neither the things that have come to pass among human beings may become faded away by time, nor great and wondrous deeds, some displayed by Greeks and others by non-Greeks, may become without fame, and also, among other matters, the cause for which they made war on one another.

Now the learned men of the Persians say that the Phoenicians became responsible for the dispute. For these people, having come from the sea called Red to this sea here, and having settled the region which they still inhabit now, at once set themselves to long sea voyages, carrying Egyptian and Assyrian cargoes and arriving both elsewhere and especially at Argos.
At that time Argos held first place among all places in the land now called Hellas. When the Phoenicians arrived at this Argos, they set out their cargo for sale.

On the fifth or sixth day after they arrived, when almost everything had been sold by them, many women came down to the sea, including the daughter of the king; her name was, according to the very same account that the Greeks also give, Io daughter of Inachus.

As these women stood by the stern of the ship, they were buying the wares for which they had the greatest desire; and the Phoenicians, after urging one another on, rushed upon them. Most of the women escaped, but Io was seized together with others. After putting them into the ship, they went off sailing away toward Egypt.

readerTranslations.translation: Here Herodotus of Halicarnassus sets out his inquiry: so that human events will not be erased by time, so that the great and astonishing deeds of Greeks and non-Greeks alike will not lose their fame, and so that the cause of their war with one another may be known.

Persian authorities say the Phoenicians were responsible for the quarrel. They had come from the sea called the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, settled the coast they still occupy, and quickly took up long-distance seafaring. Carrying Egyptian and Assyrian goods, they traded in many places, including Argos.
At that time Argos was the leading place in the land now called Greece. When the Phoenicians reached Argos, they displayed their cargo for sale.

On the fifth or sixth day after their arrival, when nearly everything had been sold, many women came down to the shore. Among them was the king's daughter, whose name, as the Greeks also say, was Io daughter of Inachus.

While the women stood near the ship's stern buying the goods that most caught their fancy, the Phoenicians gave one another the word and rushed at them. Most escaped, but Io and some others were seized, thrown aboard, and carried off by ship toward Egypt.

illustrationPromptSeed.style: Ionian field notebook: reed-pen linework, sea-weathered blues, red-figure silhouette accents, clear map labels, consistent traveler-narrator presence.
continuityNotes: Keep Herodotus as a recurring traveler-recorder: bearded Ionian Greek, plain mantle, wax tablets or papyrus roll, observational rather than heroic pose.
Use the same sea-weathered blue wash and red-figure accents planned for the world-classics-seed Herodotus sequence.
Treat Io and the Phoenician traders as early mythic-history figures, not fantasy characters; avoid anachronistic ships, clothing, or weapons.
illustrationPromptSeed.prompt: Herodotus opens his inquiry as a field notebook spread: on one side, an Ionian recorder from Halicarnassus writes beside a labeled map of the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean; on the other, Phoenician traders at Argos display Egyptian and Assyrian cargo near a ship stern as Io and other women approach. Reed-pen linework, sea-blue washes, restrained red-figure silhouettes, clear labels for Halicarnassus, Argos, Phoenicia, Egypt, and the sea routes; documentary tone, no modern objects, no fantasy effects.

uncertainties: `ἱστορίης ἀπόδεξις` is programmatic: `presentation of inquiry`, `display of research`, and `publication of investigation` are all possible. The reader translation uses `sets out his inquiry` for fluency.
`βαρβάροισι` means non-Greek speakers or foreigners in this context. `Non-Greeks` was used in the reader translation to avoid an unnecessary modern pejorative tone.
`τῆς Ἐρυθρῆς ... θαλάσσης` is literally the Red Sea, but Herodotus can use the term broadly for waters beyond the Near East, including the Persian Gulf or Indian Ocean region.
`τήνδε τὴν θάλασσαν` is literally `this sea here`; the reader translation interprets it as the Mediterranean from the narrator's geographical frame.
`λόγιοι` is rendered as `learned men` and `authorities`; it means people versed in accounts, not necessarily official historians.
The infinitives in 1.1.1-1.1.4 continue the indirect discourse governed by `φασί`; these events are presented as the Persian version of the quarrel.
`διακελευσαμένους` may mean the Phoenicians urged one another on or gave one another a signal. The reader translation chooses `gave one another the word`.
